name: Local Neighbourhood (Science Fiction)
description: The same real stars as the Local Neighbourhood map, at their true positions — but populated with the famous science fiction set among them. Sol runs on The Expanse; Pandora circles Alpha Centauri A; Reach guards Epsilon Eridani; the Nostromo is still answering that beacon at Zeta Reticuli. This map is deliberately fictional: the planets, stations and ships come from the novels, films and games, not from the catalogues. Stars without a famous fictional tenant keep their real confirmed planets.

nodes.name: Sol
nodes.description: Sol, a couple of centuries on: Earth and Mars glare at each other across the gravity well while the Belt does the actual work. Ceres and Eros anchor the Belt economy, Tycho Station builds the impossible, and something very old and very patient has just been dug out of Phoebe. Remember the Cant.

nodes.name: Mercury
nodes.description: The smallest planet and closest to the Sun. Mercury is a world of extremes, with scorching daytime temperatures (430°C) and frigid nights (-180°C). It has no real atmosphere, only a thin exosphere, and its cratered surface resembles Earth's Moon.

nodes.name: Venus
nodes.description: Earth's 'sister planet' in size, but a hellish world. Venus suffers from a runaway greenhouse effect, trapping heat under a thick, toxic atmosphere of CO2 and sulfuric acid clouds. Its surface pressure is 92 times that of Earth, and it's the hottest planet in the system.

nodes.name: Earth
nodes.description: The third planet from the Sun and the only known astronomical object to harbor life. It is an ocean world, with 71% of its surface covered in liquid water, protected by a strong magnetic field and a breathable nitrogen-oxygen atmosphere.

nodes.name: Luna
nodes.description: Earth's only natural satellite and the largest relative to its host planet in the Solar System. It is tidally locked, always showing the same face to Earth. Its cratered, airless surface is composed of dark volcanic 'maria' and bright, ancient highlands.

nodes.name: Mars
nodes.description: The fourth planet, known as the 'Red Planet' due to iron oxide (rust) on its surface. It's a cold desert world with a very thin CO2 atmosphere, polar ice caps, and the largest volcano (Olympus Mons) and canyon (Valles Marineris) in the Solar System.

nodes.name: Phobos
nodes.description: The larger and innermost of Mars's two moons. It is a small, lumpy, and heavily cratered body, thought to be a captured asteroid. Phobos orbits so close to Mars that it will either crash into the planet or be torn apart into a ring in about 50 million years.

nodes.name: Deimos
nodes.description: The smaller and outer of Mars's two moons. Like its sibling Phobos, Deimos is a small, dark, and irregularly shaped body, likely a captured C-type asteroid. Its surface is smoother than Phobos's, as many of its craters are filled with fine dust (regolith).

nodes.name: The Main Belt
nodes.description: A torus-shaped region of space between Mars and Jupiter, occupied by millions of asteroids. This is leftover material from the early Solar System that was prevented from forming a planet by Jupiter's immense gravity. The largest object in the belt is the dwarf planet Ceres.

nodes.name: Jupiter
nodes.description: The fifth planet and the largest in the Solar System. This gas giant is more than twice as massive as all other planets combined. It's known for its colorful cloud bands of ammonia ice and the Great Red Spot, a giant storm that has raged for centuries.
nodes.orbitalStabilityDetails: Metastable; generally long-lived (>100 Myr to Gyr), but dynamically packed and perturbation-sensitive. Drivers: Marginal Hill spacing (Delta=7.95).

nodes.name: Jupiter's Rings
nodes.description: A faint ring system composed of three main parts: an inner 'halo', a bright 'main' ring, and an outer 'gossamer' ring. Unlike Saturn's icy rings, Jupiter's are made of small, dark dust particles, likely kicked up from its small inner moons by meteoroid impacts.

nodes.name: Io
nodes.description: The innermost Galilean moon, Io is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System. It is caught in a tidal 'tug-of-war' between Jupiter and the other moons, which flexes its interior and powers hundreds of volcanoes that erupt sulfur and lava.

nodes.name: Europa
nodes.description: A smooth, ice-covered world with a young surface crisscrossed by cracks and streaks. It is a prime candidate for life, as evidence strongly suggests a deep, liquid saltwater ocean exists beneath its 15-25 km thick ice shell, kept warm by tidal heating.

nodes.name: Ganymede
nodes.description: The largest moon in the Solar System, even larger than the planet Mercury. Ganymede is a differentiated icy world and is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field. Its surface has both dark, ancient, cratered regions and lighter, younger, grooved terrain.

nodes.name: Callisto
nodes.description: The outermost Galilean moon, Callisto has the oldest and most heavily cratered surface in the Solar System, indicating a lack of geological activity. It is a geologically 'dead' world, composed of roughly equal parts rock and ice. It may also hide a subsurface ocean.

nodes.name: Saturn
nodes.description: The sixth planet and the second-largest, Saturn is a gas giant famous for its spectacular ring system. It is the least dense planet—it would float in water. Its atmosphere is a pale yellow, striped with bands of ammonia ice clouds and powerful winds.
nodes.orbitalStabilityDetails: Metastable; generally long-lived (>100 Myr to Gyr), but dynamically packed and perturbation-sensitive. Drivers: Marginal Hill spacing (Delta=7.95).

nodes.name: Saturn's Rings
nodes.description: The most extensive and complex ring system in the Solar System. The rings are not solid but are made of billions of particles of water ice, with some rock and dust, ranging in size from a grain of sand to a house. They are incredibly thin, perhaps only 10 meters thick.

nodes.name: Titan
nodes.description: Saturn's largest moon and the only moon with a thick, Earth-like atmosphere (though it's 95% nitrogen and toxic). Its surface is -179°C, cold enough for liquid methane and ethane to form rivers, lakes, and seas in a 'hydrological' cycle similar to Earth's water cycle.

nodes.name: Enceladus
nodes.description: A small, bright white icy moon that is one of the most compelling places to search for life. It ejects massive plumes of water, ice, and organic molecules from 'tiger stripes' near its south pole, revealing a global subsurface ocean of liquid saltwater.

nodes.name: Tethys
nodes.description: A mid-sized moon of almost pure water ice — one of the most reflective bodies in the solar system. Scarred by the enormous Odysseus crater and the vast Ithaca Chasma canyon. It holds Mimas in a 2:1 orbital resonance.

nodes.name: Dione
nodes.description: An ice moon streaked with bright wispy chasms over a possible deep internal ocean. Its 2:1 orbital resonance with Enceladus is the engine that keeps pumping that smaller moon's eccentricity — and so its famous geysers.

nodes.name: Mimas
nodes.description: The smallest and innermost of Saturn's major moons, Mimas is nicknamed the 'Death Star' moon. It is dominated by the Herschel crater, a massive impact basin 139 km wide—nearly a third of the moon's own diameter—that almost shattered the icy body.

nodes.name: Rhea
nodes.description: Saturn's second-largest moon, Rhea is a heavily cratered, airless body of ice and rock. Its surface is ancient, with one hemisphere being brighter and more cratered than the other. Its surface also features bright, 'wispy' streaks, which are exposed ice cliffs.

nodes.name: Iapetus
nodes.description: Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon, Iapetus is famous for its dramatic two-tone coloration. Its leading hemisphere is as dark as coal, while its trailing hemisphere is as bright as fresh snow. It also possesses a massive, 20-km-high equatorial ridge.

nodes.name: Uranus
nodes.description: The seventh planet, an ice giant tipped on its side. Uranus rotates at a 98-degree angle, likely from a past collision, causing extreme seasons where its poles face the Sun for 42 years at a time. Its blue-green color comes from methane in its H-He atmosphere.

nodes.name: Uranus' Rings
nodes.description: Uranus is surrounded by 13 known rings. Unlike Saturn's bright, icy rings, these are extremely dark and narrow, composed of particles as dark as coal, likely water ice mixed with radiation-processed organic compounds. They were the first to be discovered after Saturn's.

nodes.name: Titania
nodes.description: The largest of Uranus's moons. This icy, rocky world shows signs of past geological activity. Its surface is cut by a system of enormous canyons and fault valleys, some stretching for 1,000 miles, indicating its interior expanded and cracked the crust long ago.

nodes.name: Oberon
nodes.description: The outermost and second-largest of the major Uranian moons. Oberon has the most ancient and heavily cratered surface of Uranus's moons, showing little sign of past geological activity. Its dark, reddish surface is covered in impact craters, some with bright rays of ice.

nodes.name: Ariel
nodes.description: The brightest and youngest-surfaced of Uranus's moons. Ariel shows clear signs of geologic activity, with vast, interconnected canyons and fault valleys. Smooth plains suggest that 'cryovolcanism' (ice volcanoes) may have once resurfaced parts of the moon.

nodes.name: Neptune
nodes.description: The eighth and most distant planet, Neptune is a dark, cold ice giant whipped by supersonic winds. It has a vivid blue color from methane in its atmosphere. It was the first planet found through mathematical prediction rather than direct observation.

nodes.name: Neptune's Rings
nodes.description: Neptune is encircled by five faint, dark rings. They are notable for containing unstable, bright clumps of dust called 'arcs,' which are thought to be held in place by the gravity of the small moon Galatea. These rings are dusty and relatively young.

nodes.name: Triton
nodes.description: Neptune's largest moon and likely a captured Kuiper Belt Object. It is one of the coldest worlds known (-235°C), yet it is geologically active, with geysers of nitrogen gas erupting from its icy surface. It orbits Neptune 'backwards' in a retrograde orbit.

nodes.name: Kuiper Belt
nodes.description: A vast, doughnut-shaped ring of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune, from about 30 to 50 AU. It is a reservoir of comets and contains many dwarf planets, including Pluto. This is a cold, distant region containing remnants from the formation of the Solar System.

nodes.name: Pluto
nodes.description: A dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt, formerly classified as the ninth planet. It is a complex world of ice mountains and frozen nitrogen plains. Its highly eccentric orbit sometimes brings it closer to the Sun than Neptune. It has five known moons.
nodes.orbitalStabilityDetails: Likely <1 kyr before major orbital disruption (collision/ejection/infall risk). Drivers: External orbit overlap with Neptune; External orbit overlap with Kuiper Belt.

nodes.name: Charon
nodes.description: Pluto's largest moon, so large (half of Pluto's diameter) that the two are considered a binary dwarf planet system. They orbit a common barycenter located in the space between them. Charon is tidally locked to Pluto, so they both always show the same face to each other.
nodes.orbitalStabilityDetails: Likely <1 kyr before major orbital disruption (collision/ejection/infall risk). Drivers: External orbit overlap with Neptune; External orbit overlap with Kuiper Belt.

nodes.name: International Space Station
nodes.description: The premier research facility in LEO. A modular habitation of modules and trusses.

nodes.name: Tiangong Station
nodes.description: A T-shaped modular station. Modern, automated, and efficient.
nodes.gmNotes: China's space station. Uses Hall Effect thrusters for station keeping.

nodes.name: Lunar Gateway
nodes.description: A small station in a Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbit around the Moon. Staging point for surface landings.
nodes.gmNotes: The bridge to the surface. High radiation environment outside.

nodes.name: Ceres
nodes.description: The largest body in the Belt and its beating heart: six million people, spun up for gravity, docks always full. The ice hauls from Saturn keep it breathing. Star Helix keeps it (mostly) honest.

nodes.name: Eros
nodes.description: A battered near-Earth asteroid with an old spin-station bored through it. Officially quarantined. Unofficially: do not approach, do not answer transmissions from it, do not ask what Protogen was doing there.

nodes.name: Phoebe
nodes.description: Saturn’s captured outer moon — captured, it turns out, from outside the system entirely, along with a passenger that waited two billion years for someone curious enough to drill.

nodes.name: Ceres Station
nodes.cargoDescription: Water ice (stolen, allegedly), Belt ore, black-market Martian military surplus, and ten thousand kilos of unlicensed coffee.
nodes.description: The port city of the Belt, tunnelled through Ceres and spun for gravity.
nodes.gmNotes: A good place to start a murder investigation. Remember the Cant.

nodes.name: Eros Station
nodes.cargoDescription: One and a half million missing persons and a radio voice that will not stop singing.
nodes.description: The oldest station in the Belt, and as of recently the fastest: Eros has started moving on its own. Nobody aboard is answering. Nobody aboard is, strictly speaking, anybody any more.
nodes.gmNotes: The protomolecule incident. Full quarantine; it may not respect that.

nodes.name: Tycho Station
nodes.cargoDescription: Half a generation ship’s worth of hull plate, and whatever Fred Johnson isn’t telling anyone about.
nodes.description: The largest mobile construction platform in the system, currently building a two-kilometre generation ship for the Mormons. What could go wrong?

nodes.name: Ganymede Agricultural Domes
nodes.cargoDescription: Soybeans, engineered yeast, and the outer planets’ entire food security.
nodes.description: The breadbasket of the outer planets, fed by orbital mirrors — and, thanks to Jupiter’s magnetosphere, canonically the safest place beyond Mars to have a baby.

nodes.name: Phoebe Research Station
nodes.cargoDescription: Core samples, biohazard containment units (all seals nominal, the logs insist), and a great deal of redacted paperwork.
nodes.description: A joint Mars-Protogen science outpost drilling into Phoebe’s ice. Contact was lost some time ago. The last data packet has been classified at a level most governments do not know exists.

nodes.name: The Sol Ring
nodes.cargoDescription: Nothing. It is a door. The cargo is whatever is foolish enough to go through.
nodes.description: A thousand-kilometre ring of protomolecule engineering, assembled just outside the orbit of Uranus after launching itself off Venus. It leads somewhere that is not here. Flight plans filed through the Ring are, at present, one hundred percent one-way.
nodes.gmNotes: Watch your speed limit inside. The slow zone is not a suggestion.

nodes.name: Rocinante
nodes.cargoDescription: Legitimate salvage (formerly MCRN Tachi). Manifest: one obsessively maintained coffee machine, assorted Martian military surplus nobody has asked for back, and a rail gun the registration paperwork does not mention.
nodes.description: A Martian corvette-class light frigate off the battleship Donnager, now flying independent under a Belter registry and a Cervantes joke. Fast, over-armed for her size, and home.
nodes.gmNotes: If the reactor is hot and her pilot is aboard, do not chase her.

nodes.name: Canterbury
nodes.cargoDescription: Saturn ring ice, 250,000 tonnes, destination Ceres — plus a shuttle called the Knight and a crew who would very much like to speak to their union rep.
nodes.description: A retrofitted colony hauler old enough to have opinions, flying the Saturn-Ceres ice run. Do not respond to distress beacons from unregistered ships. Seriously.
nodes.gmNotes: CA-2216862 is not on the flight plan. It will be.

nodes.name: Alpha Centauri System Barycentre
nodes.description: The nearest system to Sol wears two futures at once: around Alpha Centauri A, the RDA’s interstellar ventures circle the gas giant Polyphemus and its garden moon Pandora; around Proxima, the slow colonisation of Per Ardua proceeds one lifetime at a time. (A third famous tenant, Trisolaris, is best not spoken of where the suns can hear.)

nodes.name: Rigil Kentaurus (Alpha Centauri A)
nodes.description: A near-twin of the Sun, slightly older and brighter. No confirmed planets yet, though candidate signals have been reported around both A and B for years.

nodes.name: Toliman (Alpha Centauri B)
nodes.description: The orange-dwarf half of the central pair. From a planet here, Alpha Centauri A would outshine the full Moon thousands of times over.

nodes.name: Proxima Centauri (Alpha Centauri C)
nodes.description: The nearest star to the Sun, and in Stephen Baxter’s telling the destination of humanity’s first, brutal one-way colony ships. Its real planets are joined here by Per Ardua, the tidally locked world where the colonists learned what "per ardua ad astra" actually costs.

nodes.name: Proxima Centauri d
nodes.description: A sub-Earth of at least a quarter of an Earth mass, skimming the star every five days. One of the lightest planets ever found by radial velocity.

nodes.name: Proxima Centauri b
nodes.description: The nearest known exoplanet: at least 1.1 Earth masses, orbiting inside the habitable zone every 11.2 days. Tidally locked and scoured by flares, but temperate enough for liquid water on the day side.

nodes.name: Polyphemus
nodes.description: A banded gas giant slightly smaller and denser than Jupiter, named for the cyclops: a single vast storm-eye stares out of its clouds. Fourteen moons; the fifth is the prize.

nodes.name: Pandora
nodes.description: The fifth moon of Polyphemus: low gravity, air that kills a human in four minutes, mountains that float on superconductor ore, and a biosphere wired into a single planetary mind. The RDA came for the unobtanium. The moon has opinions about that.

nodes.name: Caliban
nodes.description: A grey outer sister of Pandora, mined briefly and abandoned: the ore veins were dead, and nothing sang there.

nodes.name: ISV Venture Star
nodes.cargoDescription: Outbound: cryosleeping contractors and one very expensive avatar programme. Return leg: sixteen tonnes of refined unobtanium at twenty million a kilo, which pays for absolutely everything else.
nodes.description: One of the RDA’s dozen interstellar vehicles on the Earth-Pandora loop: antimatter engines, photon sail, 0.7c cruise, six years each way. The most valuable machine humanity has ever built, hauling the most valuable rock it has ever found.

nodes.name: Barnard's Star
nodes.description: Robert L. Forward’s Rocheworld: the nearest single star hosts a double planet — two worlds eighty kilometres apart, sharing one atmosphere, locked in a permanent gravitational waltz. The laser-sail ship Prometheus took twenty years to get here, and the ocean lobe’s surf-loving mathematicians were worth every one of them. Barnard’s four real planets keep their orbits below.

nodes.name: Barnard d
nodes.description: Confirmed 2025 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 0.26 Earth masses. Measured radius 0.69 Earth radii. Orbital period 2.3 days.

nodes.name: Barnard b
nodes.description: Confirmed in 2024 by ESPRESSO after decades of false alarms around this star: a sub-Earth of about a third of an Earth mass on a 3.15-day orbit.

nodes.name: Barnard c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2025 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 0.34 Earth masses. Measured radius 0.74 Earth radii. Orbital period 4.1 days.

nodes.name: Barnard e
nodes.description: Confirmed 2025 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 0.19 Earth masses. Measured radius 0.64 Earth radii. Orbital period 6.7 days.

nodes.name: Rocheworld Barycentre
nodes.description: The shared centre of the double planet: two egg-shaped lobes pointing at each other, close enough to trade weather.

nodes.name: Rocheworld: Roche
nodes.description: The dry lobe: bare rock stretched into an egg by its partner’s pull. When the lobes swing close, the shared atmosphere howls across the gap.

nodes.name: Rocheworld: Eau
nodes.description: The ocean lobe, home of the Flouwen: blob-bodied geniuses who derive orbital mechanics between waves and surf hundred-metre tidal breaks for fun. First contact involved surfing lessons.

nodes.name: Gargantua
nodes.description: The system’s gas giant from Forward’s later novels, with a family of moons worth a mission each.

nodes.name: Zulu
nodes.description: An ice-covered ocean moon whose under-ice natives — the icerugs — are gardeners, geometers, and occasionally cannibals. Explored in Ocean Under the Ice.

nodes.name: Zuni (Eden)
nodes.description: The habitable moon the crew ended up marooned on — and then, on reflection, chose. Renamed Eden by people who had earned the right.

nodes.name: Prometheus
nodes.cargoDescription: Landers Eagle and Dragonfly, twenty years of consumables, and a pharmacy of No-Die: the drug that kept the crew young and slightly stupid all the way here. Side effects include the entire plot.
nodes.description: A laser-pushed lightsail ship on a one-way twenty-year cruise at a fifth of lightspeed, decelerated by Forward’s own staged-sail trick — the physics is real enough to cite.

nodes.name: Wolf 359 (CN Leonis)
nodes.description: Stardate 44002.3: forty Starfleet ships massed here to stop a single Borg cube, and thirty-nine of them died. The debris field still orbits the little red star — hulls, escape pods, eleven thousand names on a wall at Starfleet Command. "The Battle of Wolf 359" is what Starfleet calls it. Everyone who was there calls it something worse.

nodes.name: The Graveyard
nodes.description: Thirty-nine broken starships in a slow, spreading ring: Melbourne, Saratoga, Yamaguchi, Tolstoy, Kyushu, Bellerophon and the rest. Salvage is prohibited. Grief is not.

nodes.name: USS Melbourne (wreck)
nodes.cargoDescription: Nothing recoverable. The command Riker never took.
nodes.description: An Excelsior-class heavy cruiser, opened stem to stern by a cutting beam. Her captain’s chair was offered to William Riker three weeks before the battle.
nodes.gmNotes: Resistance was, on this occasion, futile.

nodes.name: USS Saratoga (wreck)
nodes.cargoDescription: Escape pod racks, all fired. One of them carried Benjamin Sisko toward a station called Deep Space Nine, and a war nobody saw coming.
nodes.description: A Miranda-class ship lost with most of her crew, including Jennifer Sisko. Her survivors’ stories did not end here.

nodes.name: Lalande 21185
nodes.description:
The brightest red dwarf in the northern sky and the fourth-closest system to Sol, with two confirmed planets from precision radial-velocity work.

A quiet, old M dwarf. It has been in star catalogues since 1801, and in planet-hunt target lists for over a century.

nodes.name: Lalande 21185 b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2019 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 2.69 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.45 Earth radii. Orbital period 12.9 days.

nodes.name: Lalande 21185 c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2021 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 13.6 Earth masses. Measured radius 3.76 Earth radii. Orbital period 8.1 years.

nodes.name: Sirius Barycentre
nodes.description: The brightest star in Earth’s sky, and — per the Guide — corporate home of the Sirius Cybernetics Corporation, whose Complaints Division now covers the major land masses of three planets and is the only part of the company to turn a consistent profit. Their motto is "Share and Enjoy". Their products are why the doors in your ship sigh at you.

nodes.name: Sirius A
nodes.description: A hot white main-sequence star, twice the Sun’s mass and twenty-five times its light. Its glare hid its tiny companion for decades after the companion’s gravity had already given it away.

nodes.name: Sirius B
nodes.description: The nearest white dwarf: a full solar mass compressed into a sphere smaller than Earth. A teaspoon of its matter would weigh several tonnes.

nodes.name: Sirius Cybernetics Complaints Division
nodes.cargoDescription: Forty million returned Genuine People Personality modules, several billion unread complaint forms, and a Nutrimatic dispenser producing a liquid almost, but not quite, entirely unlike tea.
nodes.description: Orbital overflow processing for the Complaints Division ("Share and Enjoy"). The ground HQ famously sank halfway into the crust, leaving its illuminated motto reading, in the local language, "Go Stick Your Head in a Pig".
nodes.gmNotes: The marketing division defines the company as "a bunch of mindless jerks who will be the first against the wall when the revolution comes". The revolution is behind schedule.

nodes.name: Luyten 726-8 Barycentre
nodes.description: A close-matched pair of red flare dwarfs. UV Ceti is the prototype flare star: its eruptions can brighten it seventy-five-fold in minutes, and the whole class now bears its name.

nodes.name: BL Ceti (Luyten 726-8 A)
nodes.description: The marginally heavier half of the pair, itself a flare star of the class its twin defines.

nodes.name: UV Ceti (Luyten 726-8 B)
nodes.description: The archetypal flare star. During a 1952 outburst it brightened by a factor of 75 in twenty seconds. A super-Neptune candidate was reported around the pair in 2024, but remains unconfirmed.

nodes.name: Ross 154 (V1216 Sagittarii)
nodes.description:
A young red flare dwarf in Sagittarius, the nearest star in that constellation. No planets have been confirmed.

A UV Ceti-type flare star, less than a billion years old, flaring roughly every two days.

nodes.name: Ross 248 (HH Andromedae)
nodes.description:
A red dwarf in Andromeda. In about 36,000 years it will overtake Alpha Centauri as the closest star system to Sol, and Voyager 2 is drifting in its general direction.

A spotted, slowly pulsing flare dwarf. Voyager 2 will pass within 1.7 light years of it in roughly 40,000 years.

nodes.name: Epsilon Eridani (Ran)
nodes.description: FLEETCOM Sector One. Epsilon Eridani is the military heart of the UNSC: Reach trains the Spartans, Tribute builds the ships, and twenty orbital defence platforms watch a sky that, one day in August 2552, will fill with Covenant. The system’s two real asteroid belts are canon and present.

nodes.name: Inner Warm Belt
nodes.description: A warm asteroid belt at about 3 AU, analogous to our Main Belt, mapped by Spitzer infrared observations.

nodes.name: Outer Warm Belt
nodes.description: A second, cooler belt near 20 AU, close to where Uranus sits at home.

nodes.name: Cold Debris Ring
nodes.description: A bright, resolved ring of icy debris spanning roughly 35 to 100 AU, the system’s Kuiper Belt analogue and one of the best-imaged debris discs in the sky.

nodes.name: Epsilon Eridani I
nodes.description: The innermost world: airless, sun-blasted, and useful mainly as a gunnery reference point.

nodes.name: Reach (Epsilon Eridani II)
nodes.description: Humanity’s fortress world: titanium mines, Sword Base, New Alexandria, the Aszod ship-breaking yards, and the SPARTAN programme’s home. Per Halo canon it will be glassed in August 2552 and partly rehabitable by 2589. Until then: Reach stands.

nodes.name: Turul
nodes.description: Reach’s larger moon, named by Hungarian settlers for the mythical falcon.

nodes.name: Csodaszarvas
nodes.description: The Miracle Stag: Reach’s second moon, home to an ONI listening post nobody talks about.

nodes.name: Tribute (Epsilon Eridani III)
nodes.description: The industrial colony: shipyards, factories and the city of Casbah. Partially glassed in 2552; resettled, because Tribute does not stay down.

nodes.name: Emese
nodes.description: Tribute’s moon, another name from the settlers’ Hungarian mythology.

nodes.name: Epsilon Eridani IV
nodes.description: A cold, thinly settled world with an insurrectionist history the UNSC would rather forget.

nodes.name: Beta Gabriel
nodes.description: A resort world, mostly wilderness. After 2552, a hiding place for Jiralhanae holdouts who did not get the message about the war ending.

nodes.name: Circumstance
nodes.description: Universities and courts of justice: where the UNSC sends its lawyers, which is its own kind of deterrent.

nodes.name: Tantalus
nodes.description: An outer colony, likely glassed in 2552. Its name was always tempting fate.

nodes.name: Anchor 9
nodes.cargoDescription: Frigate spare parts, MAC rounds, and an entire Sabre programme that officially does not exist.
nodes.description: A UNSC orbital repair and refit dock over Reach, one of twenty defence platforms in the sky the night the Covenant came.

nodes.name: UNSC Pillar of Autumn
nodes.cargoDescription: One (1) shipboard AI, Cortana. One (1) SPARTAN-II in cryo. Contents fragile. Do not open until Halo.
nodes.description: A refitted Halcyon-class cruiser holding station over Reach, fuelled and provisioned for a mission nobody aboard has been briefed on. Cole Protocol in effect: if it falls back, its jump will be random. That randomness is about to make history.

nodes.name: Lacaille 9352 (GJ 887)
nodes.description:
The brightest red dwarf in the southern sky and an unusually calm one, hosting four confirmed planets including two super-Earths found by the RedDots campaign.

A remarkably quiet M dwarf: almost no starspots and very rare flares, which makes its planets unusually pleasant real estate by red-dwarf standards.

nodes.name: Lacaille 9352 e
nodes.description: Confirmed 2026 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.46 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.12 Earth radii. Orbital period 4.4 days.

nodes.name: Lacaille 9352 b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2020 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 3.9 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.8 Earth radii. Orbital period 9.3 days.

nodes.name: Lacaille 9352 c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2020 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 6.5 Earth masses. Measured radius 2.43 Earth radii. Orbital period 21.8 days.

nodes.name: Lacaille 9352 d
nodes.description: Confirmed 2026 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 6.1 Earth masses. Measured radius 2.34 Earth radii. Orbital period 50.8 days.

nodes.name: Ross 128 (FI Virginis)
nodes.description:
A quiet, old red dwarf hosting Ross 128 b: a temperate Earth-sized planet, and one of the nearest potentially habitable worlds known.

An ageing red dwarf that has largely outgrown its flaring youth, to the great benefit of its planet.

nodes.name: Ross 128 b
nodes.description: At least 1.4 Earth masses on a 9.9-day orbit, receiving 38% more light than Earth. Its quiet host makes it one of the best nearby candidates for a temperate, survivable surface.

nodes.name: EZ Aquarii System Barycentre
nodes.description: A cramped triple of red flare dwarfs: an inner pair whirling around each other every four days, orbited by a third star two astronomical units out.

nodes.name: EZ Aquarii Aa
nodes.description: The primary of the inner spectroscopic pair.

nodes.name: EZ Aquarii Ab
nodes.description: Locked in a 3.8-day embrace with its primary; the two stars are separated by only a few stellar diameters.

nodes.name: EZ Aquarii B
nodes.description: The outer member, circling the inner pair every 2.3 years.

nodes.name: Procyon Barycentre
nodes.description: Per the Star Charts, the Procyon system hosts Andor: a ringed gas giant whose ice-moon Andoria raised one of the Federation’s founding species. (Older charts filed Andoria under Epsilon Indi; the Andorians decline to settle the matter for you, and consider the argument itself excellent sport.)

nodes.name: Procyon A
nodes.description: One and a half solar masses and nearly seven times the Sun’s light: a star burning through its fuel fast, already puffing up into subgianthood.

nodes.name: Procyon B
nodes.description: A cool, ancient white dwarf that finished dying over a billion years ago. Its existence was deduced from Procyon A’s wobble in 1840, half a century before a telescope caught it.

nodes.name: Andor
nodes.description: A ringed gas giant in Procyon’s cold outer reaches, bright in Andoria’s sky through every long winter — which is all of them.

nodes.name: Rings of Andor
nodes.description: Broad ice rings; Andorian poetry insists they are the frozen breath of the first clan-mothers.

nodes.name: Andoria
nodes.description: An ice-bound Class M moon: surface cities are for tourists and the brief summer’s minus twenty-eight; real Andorian life happens in the geothermal warrens below. Home of the Andorians and the Aenar, founding members of the Federation, antennae and all.

nodes.name: 61 Cygni Barycentre
nodes.description: Hal Clement’s Mesklin orbits 61 Cygni A: the genre’s most famous heavy-gravity world, a discus-shaped super-giant spinning in under eighteen minutes, with three gravities at the equator and several hundred at the poles. Captain Barlennan and his centimetre-tall crew sail its methane seas, hauling human science for a fee. Hard SF does not come harder.

nodes.name: 61 Cygni A
nodes.description: The brighter of the "Flying Star" pair, so nicknamed for its then-record proper motion across the sky.

nodes.name: 61 Cygni B
nodes.description: The cooler companion, orbiting once every seven centuries. Both stars are visible together in binoculars.

nodes.name: Mesklin
nodes.description: Several thousand Earths of collapsed matter spinning every 17.9 minutes: a world flattened into a discus, where gravity runs from 3g at the rim to nearly 700g at the poles. The natives are 40-centimetre armoured centipedes with a healthy terror of falling and a magnificent gift for commerce. Ask for Captain Barlennan; bring trade goods.

nodes.name: Struve 2398 Barycentre
nodes.description: A wide pair of red dwarfs in Draco. In 2024 the primary yielded a confirmed sub-Earth planet, one of the lightest ever found around a nearby star.

nodes.name: Struve 2398 A (GJ 725 A)
nodes.description: The primary, a mid-M dwarf with a compact confirmed planet found by ESPRESSO radial velocities.

nodes.name: Struve 2398 A b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2025 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 2.78 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.48 Earth radii. Orbital period 11.2 days.

nodes.name: Struve 2398 B (GJ 725 B)
nodes.description: The smaller twin, a flare star catalogued as HD 173740.

nodes.name: Groombridge 34 Barycentre
nodes.description: A wide binary of red dwarfs in Andromeda. The primary hosts two confirmed planets: a hot super-Earth and a cold long-period companion.

nodes.name: Groombridge 34 A (GX Andromedae)
nodes.description: A quiet M2 dwarf with a confirmed two-planet system spanning from an 11-day orbit out beyond the snow line.

nodes.name: Groombridge 34 A b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2014 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 3.03 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.55 Earth radii. Orbital period 11.4 days.

nodes.name: Groombridge 34 A c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2018 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 36 Earth masses. Measured radius 6.67 Earth radii. Orbital period 20.8 years.

nodes.name: Groombridge 34 B (GQ Andromedae)
nodes.description: The faint secondary, a flare dwarf orbiting on a long, notably eccentric path around its partner.

nodes.name: DX Cancri
nodes.description:
One of the smallest true stars known: a red dwarf right at the edge of the hydrogen-burning limit, shining with a fifteen-hundredth of the Sun’s light.

A flare star that can quintuple in brightness. Any dimmer and it would have been born a brown dwarf instead.

nodes.name: Epsilon Indi System Barycentre
nodes.description: An orange dwarf trailed at 1,500 AU by a pair of brown dwarfs, and home to Epsilon Indi Ab: the nearest Jupiter-like planet ever directly imaged, photographed by JWST in 2024.

nodes.name: Epsilon Indi A
nodes.description: A bright K dwarf with a cold Jupiter and a pair of brown dwarfs for company. The 1975 Star Fleet Technical Manual charted Andoria here; the modern Star Charts moved it to Procyon, where this map keeps it. TOS canon does record Epsilon Indi being raided by marauders centuries back — so its quiet real planets may have stories.

nodes.name: Epsilon Indi A b
nodes.description: A cold gas giant of several Jupiter masses on a decades-long orbit, directly imaged by JWST in 2024. The nearest imaged exoplanet to Earth.

nodes.name: Epsilon Indi Ba
nodes.description: The heavier of the closest known binary brown-dwarf pair to Earth: a T dwarf glowing with its own fading heat of formation.

nodes.name: Epsilon Indi Bb
nodes.description: The cooler twin, a methane-atmosphere T dwarf about the temperature of a hot oven.

nodes.name: Tau Ceti
nodes.description: Every Astrophage-infected star in the local cluster is dimming — Sol included. Tau Ceti alone is not, and finding out why is the whole mission: a crewed suicide run in a ship named Hail Mary, and the answer lives in the clouds of the planet Adrian. Also present: a visiting engineer from 40 Eridani with five arms, a xenonite hull, and excellent jazz hands.

nodes.name: Tau Ceti g
nodes.description: Confirmed 2017 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.75 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.18 Earth radii. Orbital period 20 days.

nodes.name: Tau Ceti h
nodes.description: Confirmed 2017 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.83 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.19 Earth radii. Orbital period 49.4 days.

nodes.name: Tau Ceti f
nodes.description: Confirmed 2017 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 3.93 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.81 Earth radii. Orbital period 1.7 years.

nodes.name: Tau Ceti Debris Disc
nodes.description: A broad, massive disc of cold debris stretching from roughly 6 to 52 AU, an oversized cousin of the Kuiper Belt.

nodes.name: Adrian
nodes.description: A hot, heavy super-Earth whose upper atmosphere hosts Taumoeba: the natural predator of Astrophage, and the reason Tau Ceti still shines. Sampling it involves a chain, a scoop, and more courage than fuel. (Its slot corresponds to the once-catalogued Tau Ceti e.)

nodes.name: Hail Mary
nodes.cargoDescription: Two million kilograms of Astrophage (spent), four data beetles — John, Paul, George and Ringo — prepped for the run home, and a crew roster of one science teacher who was not supposed to wake up first.
nodes.description: Earth’s last-throw interstellar ship, Astrophage-fuelled, crewed by whoever survived the coma. Currently orbiting Adrian and doing science with whatever is to hand. Amaze, Amaze!

nodes.name: Blip-A
nodes.cargoDescription: Xenonite hull stock, tools for every conceivable emergency, a large supply of hot high-pressure ammonia, and one grieving, brilliant engineer. Amaze, question?
nodes.description: The Eridian ship from 40 Eridani, named by the human who saw it as a blip on radar. Sole survivor aboard: Rocky, engineer, last of a crew of twenty-three who never discovered radiation until it found them.

nodes.name: YZ Ceti
nodes.description:
A red flare dwarf with three confirmed rocky planets, all orbiting closer to their star than Mercury does to the Sun. The innermost may be broadcasting: it is a candidate for radio emission driven by its magnetic interaction with the star.

A small flare star only a few hundredths of the Sun’s brightness, whirling three Earth-sized planets through week-long years.

nodes.name: YZ Ceti b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2017 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 0.7 Earth masses. Measured radius 0.91 Earth radii. Orbital period 2 days.

nodes.name: YZ Ceti c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2017 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.14 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.05 Earth radii. Orbital period 3.1 days.

nodes.name: YZ Ceti d
nodes.description: Confirmed 2017 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.09 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.03 Earth radii. Orbital period 4.7 days.

nodes.name: GJ 1061
nodes.description:
An unassuming red dwarf that turned out to host three super-Earths, one of them orbiting squarely in the habitable zone.

A low-activity M dwarf, overlooked for a century until the RedDots campaign teased three planets out of its wobble.

nodes.name: GJ 1061 b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2020 (radial velocity). Mass 1.11 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.04 Earth radii. Orbital period 3.2 days.

nodes.name: GJ 1061 c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2020 (radial velocity). Mass 1.81 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.19 Earth radii. Orbital period 6.7 days.

nodes.name: GJ 1061 d
nodes.description: A super-Earth of at least 1.6 Earth masses receiving Mars-like insolation: comfortably inside the habitable zone if it holds any reasonable atmosphere.

nodes.name: Luyten's Star (GJ 273)
nodes.description:
A quiet red dwarf with two confirmed planets, including the temperate super-Earth Luyten b, long rated among the most habitable-zone-friendly worlds within twenty light years. It sits barely a light year from Procyon in real space.

A slow-rotating, placid M dwarf. From its planets, Procyon would blaze as a beacon far brighter than Venus does from Earth.

nodes.name: Luyten c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2017 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.18 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.06 Earth radii. Orbital period 4.7 days.

nodes.name: Luyten b
nodes.description: A super-Earth of at least 2.9 Earth masses in the habitable zone, target of the 2017-18 "Sonar Calling GJ 273b" interstellar radio transmission from Earth.

nodes.name: Teegarden's Star
nodes.description:
A feeble, ancient red dwarf missed by every survey until 2003, now known to host three temperate planets. Teegarden b holds one of the highest Earth-similarity ratings of any known world.

One of the dimmest stars on this map, radiating well under a thousandth of the Sun’s light. Its three confirmed planets huddle within a twentieth of Earth’s orbital distance.

nodes.name: Teegarden b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2019 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.16 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.05 Earth radii. Orbital period 4.9 days.

nodes.name: Teegarden c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2019 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.05 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.02 Earth radii. Orbital period 11.4 days.

nodes.name: Teegarden d
nodes.description: Confirmed 2024 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 0.82 Earth masses. Measured radius 0.95 Earth radii. Orbital period 26.1 days.

nodes.name: Kapteyn's Star
nodes.description:
A visitor from another galaxy: a halo red dwarf on a retrograde orbit, likely torn from the Omega Centauri progenitor dwarf galaxy eleven billion years ago. It hosts one confirmed planet nearly as old as the universe’s first stars.

A metal-poor subdwarf moving backwards around the galaxy relative to nearly every star you can see: debris from a galaxy the Milky Way consumed long before the Sun existed.

nodes.name: Kapteyn c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2014 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 7 Earth masses. Measured radius 2.54 Earth radii. Orbital period 0.3 years.

nodes.name: Kruger 60 Barycentre
nodes.description: A close binary of red dwarfs in Cepheus, orbiting each other about as far apart as the Sun and Saturn. The secondary is a well-studied flare star.

nodes.name: Kruger 60 A
nodes.description: The primary: a quarter of a solar mass, orbited closely enough by its twin that the pair complete a lap within a 45-year human working lifetime.

nodes.name: Kruger 60 B (DO Cephei)
nodes.description: A flare star that doubles in brightness every few hours of observation on average.

nodes.name: SCR 1845-6357 Barycentre
nodes.description: A red dwarf at the very bottom of the stellar mass ladder, orbited at Jupiter-ish distance by a directly imaged T-type brown dwarf.

nodes.name: SCR 1845-6357 A
nodes.description: Barely a star: a late-M dwarf discovered only in 2004, despite being one of our two dozen nearest neighbours.

nodes.name: SCR 1845-6357 B
nodes.description: A methane brown dwarf imaged at about 4 AU from its primary, glowing only in the infrared.

nodes.name: WISE 0855-0714
nodes.description:
The coldest known object outside a planetary system, and the fourth-closest system to Sol: a rogue Y-class brown dwarf far colder than a winter’s day, with water-ice clouds in its atmosphere.

A free-floating world of a few Jupiter masses, discovered by the WISE infrared survey in 2014. At about -25 degrees Celsius it is colder than Earth’s poles, yet it formed like a star.

nodes.name: Wolf 1061
nodes.description:
A quiet red dwarf with three confirmed super-Earths, including Wolf 1061 c on the inner edge of the habitable zone.

A low-activity M dwarf whose three planets were teased out of two decades of HARPS spectra.

nodes.name: Wolf 1061 b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2015 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.91 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.21 Earth radii. Orbital period 4.9 days.

nodes.name: Wolf 1061 c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2015 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 3.41 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.66 Earth radii. Orbital period 17.9 days.

nodes.name: Wolf 1061 d
nodes.description: Confirmed 2015 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 7.7 Earth masses. Measured radius 2.69 Earth radii. Orbital period 0.6 years.

nodes.name: GJ 9066 (TZ Arietis)
nodes.description:
A faint red flare dwarf (TZ Arietis) hosting a confirmed gas giant on a long orbit: a genuine cold Jupiter around one of the smallest stars known to have one.

A dim, flaring M dwarf. Its cold giant planet is an oddity: stars this light rarely manage to build one.

nodes.name: GJ 9066 c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2020 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 66.74 Earth masses. Measured radius 9.6 Earth radii. Orbital period 2.1 years.

nodes.name: GJ 674
nodes.description:
A young, active red dwarf with one confirmed close-in planet, found by HARPS in 2007 among the first low-mass worlds ever detected.

An M dwarf young enough to still carry strong magnetic activity; its hot Neptune-mass planet whips round in under five days.

nodes.name: GJ 674 b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2007 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 11.09 Earth masses. Measured radius 3.33 Earth radii. Orbital period 4.7 days.

nodes.name: GJ 687
nodes.description:
A red dwarf in Draco with two confirmed Neptune-mass planets, one temperate and one cold.

One of the brightest M dwarfs in the northern sky, visible in amateur telescopes, with a two-Neptune planetary system.

nodes.name: GJ 687 b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2014 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 17.2 Earth masses. Measured radius 4.32 Earth radii. Orbital period 38.1 days.

nodes.name: GJ 687 c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2020 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 16 Earth masses. Measured radius 4.14 Earth radii. Orbital period 2 years.

nodes.name: GJ 876
nodes.description:
A red dwarf carrying four confirmed planets locked in a celebrated 1:2:4 Laplace resonance chain: the first extrasolar echo of Jupiter’s Galilean moons, and the first M dwarf ever found to host a planet.

A modest M dwarf with an immodest planetary system: two giants and a super-Earth marching in exact 1:2:4 resonance, plus a hot inner world. Planet-hunting history was made here repeatedly between 1998 and 2010.

nodes.name: GJ 876 d
nodes.description: One of the first known super-Earths (2005): about 6.8 Earth masses, racing round its star in under two days.

nodes.name: GJ 876 c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2000 (radial velocity). Mass 0.71 Jupiter masses. Measured radius 14 Earth radii. Orbital period 30.1 days.

nodes.name: GJ 876 b
nodes.description: A two-Jupiter-mass giant on a 61-day orbit: the first planet ever confirmed around a red dwarf (1998).

nodes.name: GJ 876 e
nodes.description: Confirmed 2010 (radial velocity). Mass 14.6 Earth masses. Measured radius 3.92 Earth radii. Orbital period 0.3 years.

nodes.name: GJ 1002
nodes.description:
A quiet red dwarf with two confirmed Earth-mass planets, both inside the habitable zone: one of the most promising nearby systems for temperate terrestrial worlds.

A small, calm M dwarf: no significant flaring, and two roughly Earth-mass planets orbiting where water could stay liquid on both.

nodes.name: GJ 1002 b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2022 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.08 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.03 Earth radii. Orbital period 10.3 days.

nodes.name: GJ 1002 c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2022 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 1.36 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.1 Earth radii. Orbital period 21.2 days.

nodes.name: GJ 832
nodes.description:
A southern red dwarf with a confirmed cold Jupiter analogue on a decade-long orbit: a miniature Solar System architecture around a small star.

A modest M dwarf in Grus. A once-claimed inner super-Earth was retracted in 2022; the outer giant survived scrutiny.

nodes.name: GJ 832 b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2008 (radial velocity). Mass 0.99 Jupiter masses. Measured radius 13.8 Earth radii. Orbital period 10.5 years.

nodes.name: GJ 682
nodes.description:
A dim red dwarf in Scorpius with two confirmed super-Earths, one of them in the habitable zone.

One of the nearest stars in Scorpius, faint enough that its two-planet system went undetected until 2014.

nodes.name: GJ 682 b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2014 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 4.4 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.93 Earth radii. Orbital period 17.5 days.

nodes.name: GJ 682 c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2014 (radial velocity). Minimum mass 8.7 Earth masses. Measured radius 2.89 Earth radii. Orbital period 57.3 days.

nodes.name: 40 Eridani System Barycentre
nodes.description: Two of science fiction’s most famous worlds share this very real triple star. Around 40 Eridani A: Erid, the crushing ammonia world of Rocky’s people — and Vulcan, because Gene Roddenberry himself endorsed this star for it in 1991 and the franchise later made it official. Live long and prosper; fist my bump. The GM may pick a canon, or run both and enjoy the border disputes.

nodes.name: 40 Eridani A (Keid)
nodes.description: A stable K dwarf with the neighbourhood’s best real-estate paradox: in one canon its second planet echolocates, in another it raises eyebrows. The white dwarf next door (the first ever discovered) makes the evening sky remarkable in both.

nodes.name: 40 Eridani B
nodes.description: The first white dwarf ever identified, and still the easiest to observe from Earth. A dead star’s core, slowly cooling for the past few billion years.

nodes.name: 40 Eridani C
nodes.description: A red flare dwarf circling the white dwarf every 233 years: a live star and a dead one keeping close company.

nodes.name: Erid
nodes.description: Home of the Eridians: 29 atmospheres of hot ammonia, gravity twice Earth’s, and air so opaque its people never saw their own stars — they built radar instead of telescopes, and starships before they discovered relativity. Population: engineers, all the way down.

nodes.name: Vulcan
nodes.description: A hot, thin-aired desert world orbiting 40 Eridani A — officially Star Trek canon since Enterprise, and endorsed by Roddenberry in a 1991 letter to Sky and Telescope. Home of logic, the IDIC, and a fondness for suppressing absolutely fascinating emotions.

nodes.name: Altair
nodes.description: Altair IV: gentle green skies, two moons’ worth of light, one philologist, his daughter, a robot of infinite politeness — and beneath it all, eight thousand cubic miles of Krell machinery still humming two hundred millennia after its builders died in a single night. They had freed themselves from instrumentality. They had forgotten the monsters from the id.

nodes.name: Altair IV
nodes.description: The fourth planet of Altair: dry, green-skied, habitable, and hollow with Krell industry. The Bellerophon expedition of 2251 ended here; its lone survivor politely suggests you leave. His subconscious insists.

nodes.name: United Planets Cruiser C-57D
nodes.cargoDescription: Standard survey stores, plus sixty gallons of genuine Kansas bourbon synthesised overnight by Robby the Robot for the ship’s cook, who asked very nicely.
nodes.description: The classic United Planets flying saucer, sent to learn the fate of the Bellerophon expedition. Currently parked on the wrong planet to be asking questions about invisible monsters.
nodes.gmNotes: Robby obeys the safeguards. The thing outside the perimeter obeys nothing.

nodes.name: Bellerophon (wreck)
nodes.cargoDescription: Vaporised, mostly. The crew tried to lift off and leave; something did not want them to.
nodes.description: The 2251 expedition ship, destroyed on departure attempt. Survivors: Dr Morbius, his daughter Altaira, and whatever walks through walls when he dreams.

nodes.name: Vega
nodes.description: The Message came from here: twenty-six prime numbers wrapped around Earth’s own first television broadcast, returned to sender with blueprints folded inside. Vega is not a homeworld — it is a junction box, a relay in a transit network older than the star itself, parked among the debris rings that made astronomers suspect something was here all along. "If it is just us, it seems like an awful waste of space."

nodes.name: Warm Inner Belt
nodes.description: A warm asteroid-belt analogue detected in the infrared, hugging the snow line.

nodes.name: Cold Debris Ring
nodes.description: The famous outer debris ring: cold dust from colliding comets, the discovery that began debris-disc astronomy.

nodes.name: The Vega Relay
nodes.cargoDescription: Eighteen hours of static, if you ask the review board. Rather more, if you ask Dr Arroway.
nodes.description: A colossal polyhedral transmitter complex of no human manufacture, drifting among Vega’s debris rings: one stop in a wormhole transit network run by nobody who is taking questions. Dormant, mostly. Listening, always.

nodes.name: Zeta Reticuli Barycentre
nodes.description: Zeta 2 Reticuli, the far frontier: a ringed gas giant, three bleak moons, and a Weyland-Yutani commercial traffic lane that should never have carried a distress beacon. LV-426 has a derelict ship, a dead pilot fused to its chair, and a cargo hold nobody should ever have opened. The Company would like to remind you that Building Better Worlds remains its solemn commitment. Crew notes: the cat gets priority boarding.

nodes.name: Zeta 2 Reticuli
nodes.description: A near-perfect solar twin. A debris disc once claimed here turned out in 2017 to be background galaxies; any planets remain undetected — officially, at least. The Company’s survey charts, of course, say otherwise.

nodes.name: Zeta 1 Reticuli
nodes.description: The slightly cooler twin, a comfortable 0.06 light years from its partner: close enough to share an origin, far enough that each would see the other only as a brilliant star.

nodes.name: Calpamos
nodes.description: The ringed giant of Zeta 2 Reticuli, glowering over three moons the franchise keeps returning to. Its rings look best from a cockpit you are about to regret occupying.

nodes.name: Rings of Calpamos
nodes.description: The wide grey rings seen from orbit in every establishing shot that ever preceded a very bad decision.

nodes.name: LV-223
nodes.description: The Prometheus destination: an Engineer military installation, hangars of urns, and a black substance that improves nothing it touches. The murals were a warning, not an invitation.

nodes.name: LV-426 (Acheron)
nodes.description: Acheron: storm-scoured, pitch-dark, and impossibly dense for its 1,200-kilometre size — 0.86g that the Company’s surveyors swear is correct on both numbers. Site of the derelict Juggernaut, its fossilised pilot, and the egg chamber. Later site of Hadley’s Hope, population 158, then 1, then 0.

nodes.name: LV-178
nodes.description: A trimonite mining rock from the novels — because the Company never met a cursed moon it would not lease.

nodes.name: Hadley's Hope
nodes.cargoDescription: Terraforming consumables, one atmosphere processor (thermonuclear, definitely fine), and a directive from the Company to check out grid reference such-and-such. What could it cost?
nodes.description: A "Shake’n’Bake" terraforming colony of 158 souls huddled under an atmosphere processor. In 2179 the Company asked them to go and look at something. They found it.
nodes.gmNotes: They mostly come at night. Mostly.

nodes.name: The Derelict (Engineer Juggernaut)
nodes.cargoDescription: Several thousand leathery eggs, best left exactly as found. Pilot not included: he has been part of the chair for a few thousand years.
nodes.description: A horseshoe-shaped Engineer ship, crashed and broadcasting the same warning on loop since before human history. The Space Jockey in the pilot chair has an exit wound where his chest used to be. The hold is full. Do not go into the hold.

nodes.name: USCSS Nostromo
nodes.cargoDescription: Automated refinery under tow: twenty million tonnes of mineral ore. One (1) ship’s cat, Jones — priority boarding. Company property throughout; crew shares payable on return. Terms and conditions apply, lethally.
nodes.description: A Weyland-Yutani commercial towing vehicle, seven crew and a cat, rerouted mid-run by a signal the Company classified as a distress call and knew was not. "Building Better Worlds."
nodes.gmNotes: MU/TH/UR 6000 has sealed orders. Ripley has a bad feeling. Both are right.

nodes.name: Luhman 16 Barycentre
nodes.description: The third-closest system to Sol, yet only discovered in 2013: a pair of brown dwarfs on the L/T boundary. Luhman 16 B’s surface has been weather-mapped, revealing patchy silicate clouds — the first weather map of any object outside the Solar System.

nodes.name: Luhman 16 A
nodes.description: An L-type brown dwarf: too light to fuse hydrogen, still glowing from the heat of its formation.

nodes.name: Luhman 16 B
nodes.description: The first object beyond the Solar System to have its weather mapped: vast silicate cloud banks rotating in and out of view every five hours.

nodes.name: TRAPPIST-1
nodes.description:
The most famous planetary system beyond our own: seven Earth-sized worlds around an ultracool dwarf, several in the habitable zone, all in a resonant chain so tight that from any one planet its neighbours loom larger than our Moon. Far beyond the rest of this map, but unmissable.

A star barely larger than Jupiter, cooler than a candle flame is hot, that will outlive the Sun by trillions of years. Its seven transiting planets are the best-measured rocky worlds outside the Solar System.

nodes.name: TRAPPIST-1 b
nodes.description: Confirmed 2016 (transit). Mass 1.37 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.12 Earth radii. Orbital period 1.5 days.

nodes.name: TRAPPIST-1 c
nodes.description: Confirmed 2016 (transit). Mass 1.31 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.1 Earth radii. Orbital period 2.4 days.

nodes.name: TRAPPIST-1 d
nodes.description: Confirmed 2016 (transit). Mass 0.39 Earth masses. Measured radius 0.79 Earth radii. Orbital period 4 days.

nodes.name: TRAPPIST-1 e
nodes.description: The density champion of the habitable zone: rocky, Earth-sized, receiving two-thirds of Earth’s sunlight. The single most-studied potentially habitable exoplanet.

nodes.name: TRAPPIST-1 f
nodes.description: Confirmed 2017 (transit). Mass 1.04 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.05 Earth radii. Orbital period 9.2 days.

nodes.name: TRAPPIST-1 g
nodes.description: Confirmed 2017 (transit). Mass 1.32 Earth masses. Measured radius 1.13 Earth radii. Orbital period 12.4 days.

nodes.name: TRAPPIST-1 h
nodes.description: Confirmed 2017 (transit). Mass 0.33 Earth masses. Measured radius 0.76 Earth radii. Orbital period 18.8 days.
